title: Redis Software install and upgrade
summary: Platform and hardware requirements, install versus bootstrap, creating the first cluster, license and trial mechanics, TLS certificates, and safe in-place or rolling upgrades with security patch flow.

blocks.body:
Redis Software (the self-managed product formerly called Redis Enterprise Software) is Redis Open Source wrapped in an operations layer: a control plane — Cluster Manager UI, REST API, and CLI tools — supervising many data-plane shards per node. This lesson is the lifecycle story an operator owns: plan the hosts, install the software, bootstrap the first cluster, license and certificate it, then upgrade without dropping writes.

## Requirements and planning

The installer assumes a clean, supported host:

- **Platforms**: RHEL 8/9, Ubuntu 20/22, and Amazon Linux 2 on AMD64 (x86_64); ARM64 is supported from Redis Software 8.0.10 on RHEL 9 and Ubuntu 22. Docker works for development and testing only.
- **Network**: static IP addresses only — nodes must stay in the cluster across reboots. Configure cluster DNS so nodes reach each other by name, and open the ports: 8443 for the Cluster Manager UI, 9443 for the REST API, 8001 for the discovery service (Sentinel-compatible), 8070 for metrics export, 53/5353 for DNS/mDNS, and 10000-19999 for database client connections. An offline installation path exists for air-gapped sites.
- **Capacity**: production needs at least three nodes (keep the count odd), a minimum of 2 cores and 8 GB RAM per node with 8+ cores and 32+ GB recommended, ephemeral storage of about 2x RAM for replication and log files, and persistent storage of about 3x RAM for snapshots and AOF. Clusters beyond 35 nodes are not supported.
- **Sizing guardrails**: keep roughly 30% of node RAM free for buffers. A single node above 65% RAM — migrate resources off it; all nodes above 70% — add a node. One node above 80% CPU — move shards; all nodes above 80% — scale out.

## Install, then bootstrap

Installation and cluster creation are two distinct steps. The exam likes this distinction.

**Install** puts a node's software in place: download the package from the Redis download center, extract the tar file, and run the install script:

```sh
tar vxf redislabs-*.tar
sudo ./install.sh
```

The software installs under `/opt/redislabs`, runs as the `redislabs` user and group, and registers its processes under a supervisor. Customization knobs exist — install directory, data and log mount points, user and group ownership — but during an upgrade you cannot change the install path or the user. `rlutil` is the bundled maintenance utility for node-level tasks such as socket path management. To remove the software, `rl_uninstall.sh` ships alongside it.

**Bootstrap** creates the cluster itself — the first node becomes the cluster. You can do it through the UI or from the command line (`rladmin cluster create`, or the REST API `POST /v1/bootstrap/create_cluster`). In the UI:

1. Browse to `https://<node-address>:8443` and accept the self-signed certificate warning.
2. Select **Create new cluster** and set the administrator email and password — these same credentials sign in to the REST API.
3. Optionally paste a license key; without one the cluster starts on a trial license.
4. Choose the cluster FQDN. It **cannot be changed after creation**, and the placeholder-style `cluster.local` blocks later DNS configuration — pick a real name for anything beyond a laptop.
5. Confirm storage paths (ephemeral and persistent), and optionally enable rack-zone awareness or private/public endpoints support.
6. Acknowledge the HTTPS certificate replacement and sign in.

Every later node installs the same package and then joins instead of creating: `rladmin cluster join nodes <existing-node> ...`.

## Licenses: trial, paid, expiry

The cluster license (cluster key) enables features and sets capacity limits. Two facts anchor the exam:

- **Trial mode**: all features enabled, limited to 30 days and 4 shards (master plus replica). The clock starts when you set up the cluster on the first node, and a trial license is generated automatically if you bootstrap without providing one.
- **One license per cluster**: a passive or cold standby cluster used for disaster recovery still needs its own license.

After a paid key is applied you cannot remove it to return to trial. You can update the key at any time — Cluster Manager UI, **Cluster > Configuration > General > License**, or the license REST API. Redis Software validates the new key against the cluster name, activation and expiration dates, shard usage and limits, and features; if validation fails, the existing key stays in effect.

What expiry actually does: you can no longer change database settings or add databases, but the cluster keeps serving, and you can still sign in and view metrics, change cluster settings (including applying a renewed key), fail over when a node fails, migrate shards between nodes, and upgrade nodes. By default a license alert fires 7 days before expiration; the threshold is configurable (the `cluster_license_about_to_expire` alert setting) so renewals land in time.

## TLS certificates

At bootstrap the cluster autogenerates self-signed certificates on the first node and copies them to every node that joins. Each has a name and a job:

- `cm` — secures the Cluster Manager UI
- `api` — secures REST API requests
- `proxy` — encrypts client-to-database connections
- `syncer` — encrypts Active-Active and Replica Of synchronization traffic
- `metrics_exporter` — secures metrics shipping to external monitoring
- `ccs_internode_encryption` / `data_internode_encryption` — control-plane and data-plane internal traffic

A few are bring-your-own: `ldap_client` for LDAP authentication, `mtls_trusted_ca` for certificate-based REST API authentication, and `sso_issuer`/`sso_service` for SSO. Any autogenerated certificate can be replaced with one signed by your own CA — plan rotation before expiry, because a lapsed UI or proxy certificate is an outage you created.

## Upgrades and patches

Cluster upgrade and database upgrade are separate operations. Databases pick a Redis version at creation and are upgraded on their own schedule; the cluster setting `redis_upgrade_policy` controls which Redis versions databases may run.

Before a cluster upgrade, on every node: run `rlcheck` and require `ALL TESTS PASSED`, confirm no node is in maintenance mode (`rladmin status` — a yellow SHARDS column means maintenance mode is on), and verify the supported upgrade path from your current version. Upgrade the cluster's primary node first.

Two methods:

- **In-place**: run the new install package on each node, one at a time, starting with the primary. Simpler, but replacing node processes briefly interrupts active connections.
- **Rolling** — the production choice for continuous availability. The extra-node method installs the new version on fresh nodes, joins them, promotes one to primary, then removes old-version nodes one at a time. The replace-node method frees a node (demote it first if it is primary), reinstalls, and rejoins with `replace_node` so it reuses its node ID.

Version-specific features only activate once the entire cluster is on the new version — the documented flow restarts the execution service (`supervisorctl restart cnm_exec`) after the final node. Databases are then upgraded to a Redis version supported by the new cluster.

Security patches ride the same path: Redis Software releases implement the latest security fixes from Redis Open Source, so the operator's job is to watch release notes and upgrade. Licensing awareness is part of the story: since Redis 7.4, Redis Open Source is dual-licensed under RSALv2 and SSPLv1, with AGPLv3 added as an option from Redis 8 — but Redis Software consumers receive patches as product releases, not source pulls.

## Exam takeaways

- Install (`install.sh` on each node) is not bootstrap (creating the cluster); extra nodes join with `rladmin cluster join`, never create.
- The admin email and password set at bootstrap also authenticate the REST API; the cluster FQDN is immutable after creation.
- Trial = 30 days, 4 shards, all features, starts at first-node setup; one license per cluster — DR standbys included; expired licenses block database changes but not failover, shard migration, or upgrades.
- Self-signed certificates (`cm`, `api`, `proxy`, `syncer`, ...) are generated at bootstrap and copied to joining nodes; replace with CA-signed ones before they expire.
- Prerequisites before any cluster upgrade: `rlcheck` clean, maintenance mode off, supported path, primary node first; rolling upgrades (extra node or replace node) are the production method for staying available.
